units: a sports coach questions her pupils about their recurring aches
a boy describes a burning feeling in his thighs two days later
that boy often gave up on the sessions at the end of the week
another pupil reports a comparable discomfort in her upper back
the coach puts these aches down to sudden demands on an unprepared muscle
she recommends a longer warm-up, starting with brisk walking
she advises closing the session with stretches free of sharp movement
after a fortnight the aches ease and absences stop rising
text: At the end of practice the coach asked her group what kept on hurting once the training was over. One boy said that his thighs burned two days later, and that he often dropped the sessions at the end of the week rather than face them. A girl in the same class had much the same trouble, though hers sat high in the back. None of this surprised the coach. Soreness, she told them, comes of asking a cold muscle to work hard before it is anywhere near ready. So she stretched the warm-up out: brisk walking first, then slow circles of the arms and shoulders, and only after that the harder work. She asked them, too, to finish every session with quiet stretching, nothing sharp and nothing forced. The group trained that way for a fortnight. The aching eased off, and the register stopped filling up with absences.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old contests were held with no measuring instrument and no markings on the ground
an elderly villager acted as judge through his word alone
the end of a game depended on the players wearing themselves out
in matches today the smallest irregularity is spotted and checked on video
sportspeople of the past began play with no muscular preparation
that lack of preparation brought repeated damage to the joints
sportspeople today set aside a sizeable part of their training for warming up
the appeal of movement and the wish to outdo others have not changed
text: Picture for a moment a sporting contest from long ago. No stopwatch, no whistle, not one chalk line anywhere on the ground. An old man from the village settled every argument that came up, and his word was the whole of the rulebook. A game ended when the players had nothing left in their legs. Set that beside a match today, where the smallest shove is caught, weighed and played back on a screen. The other gap is preparation. Players once walked straight into a game with their muscles cold, and they paid for the hurry with joints that gave way again and again. Anyone who plays now gives a serious slice of every session to waking the body up before asking anything of it. One thing has not shifted, mind you: the pull of running about, and the itch to beat the person alongside you.

units: three signs give warning that an effort is outrunning the resources available
the involuntary clenching of a muscle comes above all from a shortage of water and minerals
a sharp pain under the ribs comes from poorly managed breathing
trembling in the legs reveals a store of energy almost spent
each of these signs calls for a different response
the first is answered by drinking and lengthening the muscle gently
the second is answered by slowing the pace and breathing more deeply
the third is answered by stopping, taking food and waiting
neglecting these warnings risks an injury that is slow to heal
text: Three separate signals tell a runner that the effort under way has outrun whatever is left in reserve. The first is cramp: a muscle clenches on its own and will not let go, usually once the water and the mineral salts have run low. The second is a stitch, that sharp jab under the ribs, which comes of breathing that has fallen out of step with the pace. The third is a shake in the legs, the mark of a body that is running on almost nothing. Each one asks for its own answer, and treating them alike only drags the recovery out. For cramp: drink, then lengthen the muscle slowly. For a stitch: ease off and pull the breath deeper. For the shaking: stop, eat something, then wait. A pause costs a few minutes. Brushing the warning aside often costs an injury that takes months to mend.

units: a smell of chalk and warm rubber fills the hall as the player comes in
this player had been left unused for the whole season
the person in charge of the team sends her on with a simple wave of the hand
her first attempts fail and she misses two catches
a deflected ball strikes the edge of the hoop and drops back high in the air
she recovers the ball after its bounce by throwing herself to the floor
her roll ends with the ball returned one-handed
the move earns her a point without altering the gap on the score
from that moment she stops staring at the floor and feels lighter
text: The hall smelled of chalk and warm rubber when the substitute stepped onto the boards. She had spent the whole season on the bench, counting other people's passes and warming her calves for nothing. After the break the man in charge sent her on with a flick of the hand, saying not a word. She hurried, and it showed: she fumbled two catches and felt the quiet close in around her. Then a ball came off a hand at the wrong angle, clipped the rim and floated up. She followed the bounce, threw herself down, rolled across her shoulder and pushed the ball back one-handed. The point was given, and the gap on the board stayed exactly where it had been. But she stopped looking at her feet. The rest of the match went by quickly, almost lightly, as though the floor had at last taken her weight.

units: the support must be pulled onto a straight limb and not a bent one
a support fitted over a bent joint slips from the first strides
the sleeve is drawn up from the lower leg without being rolled
a fold of fabric hinders the circulation and numbs the end of the limb
the opening in the middle must ring the kneecap without pressing on it
weight resting straight on the bone brings on a dull ache after exercise
the straps are tightened working from the bottom upwards
tightening done the other way round makes the lower joint of the leg swell
wearing it for long stretches without cause weakens the muscles concerned
text: Pull the support on with the leg held straight, never with the joint bent. Fitted over a bend, it works loose within the first few strides and holds nothing at all. Draw the sleeve up from the lower leg, smoothing it as you go, and do not roll it: a ridge of fabric presses on the vessels underneath and leaves the foot numb. Check that the opening in the middle rings the kneecap without resting on it, since weight sitting straight on the bone brings on a dull ache once the session is over. Now pull the straps in, working upwards from the lowest of them. Fastened the other way round, they drive the blood downwards and the ankle swells up. Take the support off as soon as you have finished. Worn for days on end with no cause, it does the work the muscles should be doing, and they weaken.

units: the management of a sports facility closes two halls for the time being
the warped coverings underfoot had caused accidents
the families of the children enrolled protested against this decision
the neighbouring bodies had no free slot available
a meeting open to the public was arranged
specialists named an old water leak as the source of the trouble
that leak made the boards lift under the impact of landings
the games played with a racquet or over a net move to a hall brought back into use
the dance and strength classes are held in a multi-purpose room
text: Two of the halls at the sports centre have been shut for the time being, after the boards warped underfoot and brought about a run of falls. Families whose children train there objected almost immediately, all the more so as not one of the clubs round about had a single free slot to offer them. A meeting was called, open to anyone who wished to come. Engineers set out what lay behind the damage: water had leaked in years earlier and had never been traced, so the timber lifted each time a landing shook the floor. The answer they settled on comes in two parts. Racquet games, and anything played over a net, move to a hall that volunteers have brought back into use. The dance and strength classes go into the multi-purpose room. The slots that were lost will be handed back to the families.

units: two kinds of surface are laid in most sports halls
these two surfaces answer differently under the weight of a foot
the floor set on flexible battens sinks slightly at each step
that floor hands part of the energy back to the leg
it spares the joints and forgives inexact landings
its pale shade keeps the marks of shoes and calls for regular upkeep
the synthetic surface grips harder and helps the push at the start
it puts up with water, with wheels rolling over it and with shoes from outdoors
it makes sliding painful and does not absorb impact
text: Most sports halls are laid with one or other of two surfaces, and a foot coming down on them meets a very different answer. Wood set on flexible battens gives a little under each step, then hands a part of that energy straight back to the leg. Awkward landings are forgiven, and the joints take far less of a beating. The pale boards keep every scuff left by a sole, which means they have to be cleaned again and again. A synthetic surface grips harder and gives a cleaner push at the start of a sprint. Water does it no harm, trolley wheels roll over it and shoes worn in from outdoors leave it untouched. What it will not do is soften a landing, and sliding across it hurts a good deal. The choice follows the use, then: a floor that cushions on one hand, sharp changes of direction on the other.

units: the writer holds that the mania for counting spoils the pleasure of physical activity
he sets out the effects of that mania one after another
he likens running to a graded test because of the devices worn on the arm
he notes that the pitting of one against another reaches even friendships
an easy outing thus turns into a contest with figures
whoever falls short of the weekly target feels at fault despite having been active
night-time rest too is put through the reading of graphs
the writer does not reject the measures but blames them for filling the whole space
he wants physical activity to remain a wish and not an obligation
text: Honestly, all of this counting has taken the fun out of moving about. Look at what it has brought about, one thing at a time. Running has turned into an exam: off you go with a device strapped to your arm, and home you come with a mark. Then comes the ranking, which has crept in everywhere, friendships included, so that an easy outing ends up as a contest with figures attached. Then the guilt: fall short of your target for the week and you feel at fault, never mind that you walked, swam and laughed with the people near you. Even sleep is fed through the graphs now, as though the night were a test to be passed. I am not saying the figures are useless. I am saying they have swallowed everything else. Moving ought to stay something you fancy doing, not a debt that hangs over you.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: this practitioner began her working life in a small local facility
there she eased the shoulders of swimmers during their training
she specialised in shoulder injuries, a field little sought after at the time
a women's side at the top level then took her on
she watched the throwing movements for a full season before stepping in
her way of going about it rested on video, on comparison and on talking things over
shoulder injuries fell within the group
she now leads the medical staff of a training centre
she puts her results down to listening to injured players and checking what they say
text: The club's physiotherapist started out at a small local pool, easing the shoulders of swimmers between lengths. Shoulder injuries were what she went on to study, at a time when hardly anyone chose that corner of the field. A women's side at the top level took her on, and she spent an entire season watching how the players threw before she put forward a single exercise. Her way of going about it raised eyebrows: she filmed, she compared, she talked things over with the squad instead of handing down instructions. Shoulder trouble within the group fell away sharply. She now runs the medical staff at a training centre and teaches those coming up behind her. She insists she invented nothing. She listened to the players in pain, then checked each complaint against what she could see.

units: the performance leaves the spectator with an unsettling feeling
the performers were trained in sport and not in the theatre
that background gives them an uncommon physical stamina
they dance for a full hour without their breathing betraying any tiredness
that reserve lends an unexpected scale to the closing part
the same background produces the flaw of the evening
trained to reach a target, they favour movements that make a show
gestures that serve no purpose, with nothing to prove, are missing from their work
the string of feats leaves no room for a pause
the audience comes away impressed but hardly moved
text: There is something unsettling about this piece, and the reason for it shows within minutes: the performers were trained on the track, not on the stage. From that background comes the great strength of the evening, a stamina of a kind you very rarely see. They dance for a full hour and the breath never once gives them away, and that held-back reserve lends the closing section a scale which technique on its own would never reach. The same background explains what is missing. Taught to aim at a target, the performers go for what shows: the high leap, the fall caught clean, the shape that draws a gasp from the seats. The gesture that proves nothing escapes them entirely. And so one feat follows another with nowhere at all to breathe. You come away admiring, and oddly little moved.
